Introduced flags variable to `fd_entry` for ZVFS implementation.

Fixes #66933

issue_context.title: libc: implement `feof()`
issue_context.body:
This was originally added as a ticket under POSIX, but `feof()` is not a POSIX function. It is from C89.

https://en.cppreference.com/w/c/io/feof

The expectation from the POSIX API is that this function is implemented as part of whatever C library is in use.
comments:
I would like to work on this.

Any advice?
@DanTGL - we probably need some ZVFS implementation of this (in fdtable.h) and a feof() wrapper in the common libc.

> @DanTGL - we probably need some ZVFS implementation of this (in fdtable.h) and a feof() wrapper in the common libc.

Ok, so the feof function in the common libc just calls the ZVFS implementation directly.
How should the file descriptor and the end-of-file indicator be handled?

I'm guessing that the end-of-file indicator is stored in the fd_entry?

Most standard libraries seem to define `FILE` as a struct containing the file descriptor, end-of-file indicator, and some other stuff.
`feof` just checks the end-of-file indicator, it doesn't modify it.

Aren't standard libraries already expected to implement `feof`?

Am I misunderstanding something?

> Most standard libraries seem to define `FILE` as a struct containing the file descriptor, end-of-file indicator, and some other stuff.

integer file descriptor? Obtained via `open()` or `_open()` or something like that?

That means they use POSIX under the hood, which is the dependency we want to remove.

> `feof` just checks the end-of-file indicator, it doesn't modify it.

That's right. I/O operations should set the EOF indicator when the end of a file has been reached. Hard to say if there needs to be a separate error bit.

> Aren't standard libraries already expected to implement `feof`?

Yes. However, many embedded C libraries conflate POSIX and ISO C (even ANSI C in this case), or make the assumption that the underlying OS has a native POSIX API.

> Am I misunderstanding something?

Not really. It's incredibly common.

The key difference here is that POSIX is optional in Zephyr, so we need to remove it from the dependency graph via an abstraction. Hence the ZVFS stuff.

So Zephyr's POSIX implementation depends on ZVFS and the ANSI C `FILE *` operations need to depend on ZVFS as well. Much of those APIs need to be syscalls too (which are kind of special in Zephyr).

The `struct fd_entry *` should be considered as Zephyr's native equivalent of `FILE *`.

I hope that helps to clarify things.

We shouldn't replace libc's feof here. That was my main concern with this patch. I'm not sure why zvfs is even pretending to offer the FILE type...
Should I just remove this from the common libc?

> We shouldn't replace libc's feof here. That was my main concern with this patch. I'm not sure why zvfs is even pretending to offer the FILE type...

How would Zephyr manage and associate integer file descriptors to `FILE` objects and vice versa, in that case, @keith-packard?

FILE objects are owned by stdio; they contain a bunch of stdio-specific state so that you can call things like getc, fprintf, fread and others. The zvfs FILE objects have no relation to any stdio implementation; I can't see how they are supposed to be used by a standard C application.

> How would Zephyr manage and associate integer file descriptors to FILE objects and vice versa, in that case?

This question is still unanswered.

I guess I could ask it differently. What interface would Picolibc prefer for the OS to perform stdio operations on FILE objects? Associate integer file descriptors with FILE objects? It can't be POSIX.

The OS cannot perform operations on FILE objects; FILE objects are the purview of the stdio implementation provided by the C library. If you want to perform stdio operations on `fs_file_t` objects, you need to make the stdio implementation inside the C library talk to the Zephyr FS layer. Right now, the only way to do that is to provide POSIX API support from Zephyr so that newlib or picolibc can use their existing POSIX paths.

Picolibc abstracts the OS interfaces so that we could provide stdio on top of `fs_file_t` objects without going through the POSIX layer. For that, we'd create a function in the Picolibc Zephyr support code which took a `fs_file_t` and created a FILE object wrapper. That FILE object would use only Zephyr native interfaces for all operations. Then we could provide an `fopen` implementation also using only Zephyr native interfaces. At that point, we'd have a C compatible stdio implementation with file system access which did not require the POSIX support layer in Zephyr.

I'm happy to write that code; it's not a huge amount of source, but it does require some knowledge of picolibc internals. Is this required to support `fileno`? This would require using fdtable instead of allowing applications to simply allocate `fd_file_t` dynamically as a consequence of calling `fopen`. Right now, fileno doesn't work on stdin/stdout/stderr, and only works when applications use fopen and the POSIX Zephyr support.

It seems like what's being proposed is an I/O interface that isn't dependent on POSIX which would be used by picolibc instead of reimplementing functions from the standard library like `feof`, if I'm understanding this correct.

If that's the case, then this should just be closed, right?
